newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC papers over cracks but braces for protests.
newsitem.headline: APEC papers over cracks but braces for protests.

text.p: APEC ministers papered over differences on Saturday and announced a united stand over a U.S. plan to free trade in information technology.

But while foreign and trade ministers of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation maintained a show of unity at their Manila meeting, leftist activists planned huge protests against APEC's goal to create the world's largest free trade zone.
Marches and protest motorcades involving thousands have been called on Sunday ahead of a summit of 18 leaders of APEC economies in Subic Bay north of the Philippine capital on Monday.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin was one of the first world leaders to arrive on Saturday.

His Sunday meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton will underline improved relations between China and the United States, Pacific powers whose bickering has overshadowed efforts to free trade and investment flows in the region.
A declaration at the end of two days of ministerial talks fell short of an outright commitment to free trade in computers, memory chips and telecommunications equipment.

U.S. trade negotiators had hoped APEC would seize the initiative on the issue ahead of the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore next month. In the end, the ministers passed the buck to the WTO, saying they supported its work to liberalise the trade.
U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor and acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky hailed the declaration.
"We think the language of endorsement is not only adequate but helpful as well as supportive," Kantor told a news conference. "We are delighted with the result."
Barshefsky said: "This is a significant agreement because it is the first time APEC has taken a stand on a WTO issue."

Back-room negotiations to cobble together the agreement exposed gaps between developed and developing nations over whether APEC should impose a trade agenda on its members or remain a loose coalition moving ahead through consensus.
It left blurred the outlines of what is intended as a free trade zone joining two billion people with 40 percent of global trade in countries from China to Chile and the United States.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad was lukewarhis endorsement of the U.S. plan. "We will support it to the extent it doesn't hurt us," he told a news conference.

Amnesty International on Saturday added its voice to unprecedented dissent swirling around the meeting by accusing Asia-Pacific nations of trampling over the rights of the poor, women and migrant workers.

"We're for APEC if it brings about justice and greater prosperity for people... but we're against it if there's a whole lot of evils associated with it," said Ross Daniels, executive committee member of the London-based group.

Diplomatic attention was focused on Sino-U.S. ties that will shape the destiny of the Pacific into the next century. Relations have been bedevilled by disputes over human rights, arms proliferation, Taiwan and trade.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said Washington would like to be able to lift sanctions on China imposed after the 1989 crackdown on democracy activists, but was not ready yet.
"We would like to reach the point where we felt there was justification to dropping the 1989 sanctions but we're not there yet. We'll continue to review the matter," he told reporters.
Meanwhile, a parallel forum of 450 of the region's top business executives boasted deals worth more than $2 billion were in the works.

Philippine President Fidel Ramos, wrenching his nation out of economic backwardness into the ranks of Asian tigers, is reaching out to transnational corporations to try to translate APEC's ambitious goals into action.

But in the run-up to the summit, to be held at the former U.S. naval base of Subic Bay north of Manila, hundreds of demonstrators took to the streets of Manila to denounce free economic exchanges across the Pacific.
They see it as a threat to jobs and a ploy by rich businesses and nations to exploit the poor, and they hoped to highlight this further with their planned protests on Sunday and Monday.
There were also concerns that leftwing groups might be planning terror attacks on U.S. nationals, including diplomats and journalists.
